nodes.summary: In an atomic congestion game each player is a unit of traffic. With affine delays the game is $(5/3, 1/3)$-smooth, so pure Nash equilibria, coarse correlated equilibria and no-regret play all cost at most $5/2$ times the optimum, against $4/3$ for nonatomic routing.
nodes.title: Atomic congestion games with affine delays

nodes.summary: Every finite game has a Nash equilibrium in mixed strategies. The two-player zero-sum case is von Neumann's minimax theorem; potential games even have pure equilibria.
nodes.title: Nash's theorem

nodes.summary: When a game is played repeatedly and every player uses a no-regret learning algorithm, the empirical distribution of play converges to the set of coarse correlated equilibria. Roughgarden's smoothness framework shows that price-of-anarchy bounds proved by a smoothness argument hold for these outcomes too, so the time-averaged social cost of no-regret play is nearly as good as that of any Nash equilibrium.
nodes.title: No-regret dynamics

nodes.summary: A game has an exact potential when one function on strategy profiles tracks every player's unilateral change of cost. Its minimisers are pure Nash equilibria and improvement paths are finite. Rosenthal's theorem makes every congestion game a potential game, and in fair cost-sharing network design the potential sandwiches the network cost within a factor $H(k)$, so the price of stability is at most $H(k)$.
nodes.title: Potential games

nodes.summary: Nonatomic routing games: infinitely many users each control a negligible amount of traffic and choose a minimum-latency path. Equilibria are Wardrop flows; they exist when latencies are continuous, they all have the same cost when latencies are nondecreasing, they cost at most $4/3$ times the optimum when latencies are affine (Pigou's network shows this is tight), and never more than an optimal routing of twice the…
nodes.title: Selfish routing and the price of anarchy
